text: ms have undergone significant shifts that reflect the changing prominence of different approaches to transformative change (Mace, 2014). When modern conservation efforts first rose to prominence in the late 1800s, structural approaches involving legislative changes and decisions prevailed, such as in the creation and governance of protected areas2. Later, knowledge co-creation and empowerment approaches gained ground. This box examines some of the most significant and transformative innovations in conservation. Although they haven’t yet halted the loss of biodiversity, these examples underscore how different approaches can interact and build on one another across time and across geographic and governance scales. From conservation without people to conservation including people Historically, nature conservation was perceived as requiring the exclusion of human presence. In some instances, this led to the displacement of local communities, with significant costs for human well-being and a disconnection of people and nature (Agrawal & Redford, 2009; Arruda, 1999; Brockington & Igoe, 2006; Mace, 2014; Massarella et al., 2021). While some conservation projects continue to exclude local populations from their traditional areas or restrict their natural resource use, this is increasingly not the case (Agrawal & Ribot, 2006; Li, 2002; Neumann, 2004; P . West et al., 2006). A pivotal turning point towards inclusivity was marked by the introduction of biosphere reserves in 1976 by UNESCO’s Man and Biosphere programme. Biosphere reserves incorporate a protected core zone, proscribed use zones around the protected core and buffer zones (Phillips, 2007). Biosphere reserves represented a key innovation in introducing the concept of protected areas with multiple objectives (case study on the Lake Tana Watershed in Ethiopia presented in Annex 3 .1), including sustainable use (Massarella et al., 2021). The biosphere reserve, or biosphere region concept gained momentum with the Convention on Biological Diversity adopted in 1992 as one of the outcomes of the Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro (Ishwaran, 2012). Now that multi-use protected areas have become more common, it is hard to recall how novel and even radical it was to have areas that were both protected and where certain human uses beyond recreation were allowed. The emergence of biosphere reserves was thus an important moment when conservation expanded from the idea of protecting nature from humans and towards the co-existence of people and nature (Mace, 2014). The European Union’s Natura 2000, a network of protected areas where human activities are allowed/encouraged under specific conditions, is an example of conservation action designated under the EU Council directive 92/43/EEC on the Conservation of natural habitats and of wild fauna and flora.

Recognizing Indigenous and local knowledge and community-based management The 1992 Convention on Biological Diversity’s Article 8(j) states that: “each contracting Party shall, as far as possible and as appropriate subject to national legislation, respect, preserve and maintain knowledge, innovations and practices of indigenous and local communities embodying traditional lifestyles relevant for the conservation and sustainable use of biological diversity and promote their wider application with the approval and involvement of the holders of such knowledge, innovations and practices and encourage the equitable sharing of the benefits arising from the utilization of such knowledge innovations and practices.” (CBD, 1992) This was one of the very first international recognitions of Indigenous Peoples and local communities and of their respective knowledge, visions and values. While this recognition took a long time to be applied worldwide, Indigenous Peoples and local communities and other stakeholders now often refer to this article to help maintain traditional lifestyles. In the decades following Elinor Ostrom’s Nobel prize-winning research on governing common-pool resources, community- based resource management (including community-based natural resource management, community-based tenure recognition, co-management including Indigenous Peoples and local communities for UNESCO World Heritage Sites and for Little Marine Management Areas) has gained prominence. Community-based natural resource management has been lauded for its potential to promote sustainable resource use while improving local livelihoods, which has the potential to transform relationships between people and nature (Jones, 2004). Even if it is difficult to assess the social and ecological impact of community-based approaches (Galvin et al., 2018), many countries have incorporated them into their natural resource management policies and strategies: Los Negros in Bolivia (Porras & Neves, 2006), Mai Ka Pō Ma (Office of Hawaiian Affairs et al., 2021), or the Scolel Té programme in Chiapas, Mexico (Plan Vivo, 2020). Recent developments: Rights for nature In 2008, Ecuador adopted the world’s first constitution recognizing the rights of nature (Espinosa, 2019). In the last decade, several additional countries have introduced a novel legal concept – granting legal personhood to non-human entities2, including nature itself (Maffei, 2022; Nadow et al., 2023).

In 2022, the Mar Menor lagoon in Spain became the first ecosystem in Europe with its own legal personality (Ley 19/2022, de 30 de Septiembre, [Page 14] THE THEMATIC ASSESSMENT REPORT ON THE UNDERLYING CAUSES OF BIODIVERSITY LOSS, DETERMINANTS OF TRANSFORMATIVE CHANGE AND OPTIONS FOR ACHIEVING THE 2050 VISION FOR BIODIVERSITY 114 Para El Reconocimiento de Personalidad Jurídica a La Laguna Del Mar Menor y Su Cuenca, 2022). Further, in 2023, marine turtles were granted legal personhood in Panama and in the Loyalty Islands, New Caledonia. While these advances align with Indigenous assertions of nature’s agency, clearly the new legal persons (i.e., the river or the turtle) will not represent themselves. Some scholars have argued that such legal actions could even have perverse influences on Indigenous identities and agendas (Coombes, 2020; Reeves & Peters, 2021). While innovation within the conservation sector can yield transformative change by benefiting both nature and people, it is crucial to note that not all initiatives claiming to be community-based or people-inclusive genuinely adhere to these principles (Doyon & Sabinot, 2014; Reed et al., 2018; Sullivan, 2006). Furthermore, some conservation-focused actions may be influenced by groups or ideologies with objectives unrelated to biodiversity and human well-being. Moreover, although environmental conservation and sustainable development2 through protected areas can lead to positive transformative change, there is also the potential for negative consequences. Many studies highlight that establishing conservation policies such as protected areas can lead to injustices and unequal social relations, at times infringing upon human rights2 (Brockington et al., 2008; Kottak, 1999; Pascual et al., 2021; P . West et al., 2006). [Page 16] THE THEMATIC ASSESSMENT REPORT ON THE UNDERLYING CAUSES OF BIODIVERSITY LOSS, DETERMINANTS OF TRANSFORMATIVE CHANGE AND OPTIONS FOR ACHIEVING THE 2050 VISION FOR BIODIVERSITY 116 The implications of a system perspective range from emphasizing the inherent and dynamic complexity of interconnected human and natural systems to seeing human agency as central in responding to environmental change and environmental crises (Brown & Westaway, 2011). Theories that emphasize dynamic complexity highlight the unpredictability of systems, the non-linearity of their dynamics and the importance of cross-scale interactions. All of these have consequences which may result in intended and unintended outcomes and limitations for governing transformative change (Flood, 2002; Miller & Page, 2008; Rotmans et al., 2001). 3.2.2 Structural approaches Structural approaches include theories in which transformative change occurs through sustainability-oriented changes in economic, social, political and cultural structures that form the rules by which societies operate. State regulations, market structures, institutions2 and governance arrangements at different levels (from communities to countries) are all examples of structures that condition and delineate societal practices. While some theories in this group focus on changes within structures, for example by changing the incentives affecting consumer behaviour, other approaches envisage a change of the structure itself. This approach assumes that current structures of formal and informal rules constitute a root cause of biodiversity loss and nature’s decline, as well as underlying a lack of equity, justice2 and unsustainability in general. Structural approaches can address both direct and indirect causes of biodiversity loss and nature’s decline, but mainly focus on the latter and its underlying structures in promoting transformative change. For example, new structures can be created to directly protect forests (e.g., incentives that use payment for ecosystem services or protected areas) or the indirect causes of deforestation could be tackled by, for example, changing structures such as trade regulations or environmental taxes. In promoting transformative change, inclusive and just processes are seen as important to ensure effective and sustainable outcomes.

text: ., incentives that use payment for ecosystem services or protected areas) or the indirect causes of deforestation could be tackled by, for example, changing structures such as trade regulations or environmental taxes. In promoting transformative change, inclusive and just processes are seen as important to ensure effective and sustainable outcomes. Recognizing that formal and informal structures provide the background to everyday decisions and practices, the actors involved in shaping and changing those structures (economic, social, political and cultural rules) include all of society. Some theories in this cluster feature top-down governance and policy changes that entail the involvement of local or national authorities. Others focus on how agents from civil society, social networks, Indigenous Peoples, social movements, youth and local communities can bring about structural changes in the norms and values that influence decisions and practices. This group of theories suggests that change occurs either through fundamental alterations within structures (e.g., State institutions, market structures, governance arrangements at different scales) or overall transformation of structures themselves. Actions include alteration of the broader political, economic, cultural and social impediments and structural constraints that can lead to exploitative production processes, overconsumption and the commodification of nature. This can be pursued by individuals or organizations by resisting social rules and practices, for example by sharing networks and through exchanges to maximize the use of existing goods in order to gradually change the influence of present economic structures (Behagel et al., 2019; Kallis, 2018). Actions to transform governance occupy a key role in this approach. Ecosystems can be managed in a way that serves human needs through partial transformations of the welfare State (Duit et al., 2016), for example by enhancing policy coherence (Persson et al., 2018) or putting the protection of nature at the core of community management of natural resources (Ostrom, 1990). Some change can be achieved within structures by, for example, changing the incentives affecting consumer behaviour, or by direct State intervention (e.g., protected areas, carbon taxes, behavioural approaches) that steer markets to safeguard nature (Alpízar et al., 2020). Changes in governance structures to promote transformative change include addressing different levels of policy (i.e., forms or systems of governance from the global to the local (Aksoy, 2014)), integration across currently ‘siloed’ governance sectors, inclusion of plural knowledges in governance processes and inclusion of citizens or affected actors (Visseren- Hamakers et al., 2021).

An example of structural approaches in action includes those involved in deliberate transformative change through designing institutions that address historical power imbalances and colonially-rooted injustices in resource management structures. Community-based and polycentric institutions (Ostrom, 2009) foster sustainable resource management2 practices that shift power towards local and/or historically/marginalized communities (Nagendra & Ostrom, 2012). This enables Indigenous Peoples and local communities to challenge unsustainable structures to include diverse knowledge systems 2, customary rules, practices and approaches and meanings associated with nature. In the transformative governance 2 literature, explicit recognition of hierarchical power relations and their effects in governance processes is seen as a prerequisite to transformative governance (Rusch et al., 2022). Structural approaches provide a variety of starting points for both governance actors and engaged citizens to promote transformative change. HOW TRANSFORMATIVE CHANGE OCCURS 117 governance arrangements, as well as norms and values, are at the core of these approaches. Theories grappling with structural change explain how social systems are created and reproduced through a synthesis of structure and agency (Annex 3 .3) and how through their actions, actors in the system can reproduce or challenge the structures that form the rules of society (Giddens, 1984). 3.2.3 Inner transformation approaches The main assumption in this approach is that the starting point for transformative change lies in the inner worlds of individuals or collectives (i.e., views). Transformative change occurs when the inner dimensions of sustainability2 (such as beliefs and values) are linked to outer dimensions (such as actions) towards sustainability-oriented views, structures and practices. Transformative change is therefore mobilized through integrative measures that link individual and collective inner worlds. This may entail an awareness of one’s own agency (O’Brien et al., 2023) and unleashing people’s potential and capacity to care, commit to and effect change for a more sustainable life (Wamsler & Osberg, 2022). The three spheres of transformation (personal, political and practical) (Annex 3 .3) provide a framework for understanding how the personal sphere shapes the way in which individuals interact with structures, power dynamics and collaborations in the political sphere (O’Brien & Sygna, 2013).

The three spheres of transformation (personal, political and practical) (Annex 3 .3) provide a framework for understanding how the personal sphere shapes the way in which individuals interact with structures, power dynamics and collaborations in the political sphere (O’Brien & Sygna, 2013). The root causes of biodiversity loss and nature’s decline most targeted by the inner transformation approach are disconnection from and domination over nature and people. Alienation from self, others and nature is considered to underpin contemporary social-ecological polycrisis2 while playing a central part on other social- ecological challenges such as colonization of nature and people, power imbalances, a sense of hopelessness, unsustainable narratives2 and paradigms of separation, unsustainable individual behaviours, as well as hegemonic narratives that have desecrated nature, turning it into a commodity. These hegemonic narratives lead to internalized messages of separation, superiority and instrumentalization in relation to nature. To uproot them, one first step is for individuals to become aware of their existence and how they are perpetuated. Transformative efforts thus focus on transformations of particular mindsets,2 beliefs, values, worldviews, paradigms, cultures2 and associated inner cognitive, emotional and relational capacities that translate into transformations in exterior worlds, such as habits, practices, governance or welfare policies. (Shrivastava et al., 2020; Wamsler, 2020) (Annex 3 .3). Actions associated with this approach include investing in relationships and working on the relationship with oneself. Relational activities that nurture human and other- than-human relationships, intra- and inter-generational relationships, self-other relationships and relationships with oneself can come from numerous domains such as environmental psychology, moral philosophy or from practices such as meaningful, sensory and emotional engagement with nature (Sheffield et al., 2022). Mindfulness, compassion training, self-awareness and inner reflexivity2 exercises, personal development and deep practices have the potential to mobilize, activate or shift individual consciousness, mindsets and values and ultimately people’s decision-making process to orientate them towards just and empathetic relationships and futures. Other mechanisms for addressing inner worlds may include developing practices of introspection in higher education and learning (Fazey et al., 2021; Woiwode, 2020) and the integration of transformative qualities/capacities and universal values (such as compassion) as explicit aims/criteria in regional, national or local performance frameworks, rather than economic growth (European Environment Agency, 2023; Wamsler & Bristow, 2022).

This literature emphasizes moving away from human-nature relationships characterized by utility, control and duality to mutually constitutive human- and more-than- human relationships (Scarano, 2024). Indigenous and local knowledge can play an important role in these theories, as these often express worldviews more representative of interconnection, balance and harmony (IPBES, 2022; Wamsler & Bristow, 2022). Bodies of knowledge on inner relationships and perspectives on oneself (e.g., positive psychology, Raymond & Raymond, 2019) and on spirituality (Ives & Kidwell, 2019) also contribute to this approach with activities that help people tap into their inner potential. This includes practices such as contemplative techniques, psychological and cognitive-behavioural based techniques, transformative facilitation, communication and coaching techniques (Wamsler, Hertog, et al., 2021; Wamsler, Osberg, et al., 2021). However, the impact of these techniques is limited at the level of individual’s views, without corresponding changes in practices and structures (Purser, 2021; Watson et al., 2023; Woroniecki et al., 2024). Theories in this approach counter this limitation by signalling that agency is better represented as distributed across individual and collective actors and actions. Inner transformation is not about fixing people’s views (Ives et al., 2023; Wamsler, Osberg, et al., 2021) but instead creating integrative measures, spaces and conditions that nurture a culture of inner development, [Page 18] THE THEMATIC ASSESSMENT REPORT ON THE UNDERLYING CAUSES OF BIODIVERSITY LOSS, DETERMINANTS OF TRANSFORMATIVE CHANGE AND OPTIONS FOR ACHIEVING THE 2050 VISION FOR BIODIVERSITY 118 mutual support and engagement. Education is an important example in this approach, that provides knowledge, spaces for deliberation and opportunities for practising civic engagement in environmental issues (Hayward, 2020). Such integration can be supported through working environments, communities of practice, social movements, aesthetics and education.

Organizations that shape mindsets are also important, including the United Nations, private, non- profit and faith-based organizations, educational institutions, citizen groups, Indigenous Peoples and local communities and people engaged in collective, embodied and reciprocal practices across the public realm. In conclusion, inner transformation for sustainability is a field of research, education and practice which recognizes the interdependence of inner and outer phenomena across views, structures and practices; the importance of addressing inner dimensions across individuals and collectives; and the potential that is latent within every human to enable transformative change. 3.2.4 Empowerment approaches This approach holds that transformative change occurs when agency and power are asserted from currently marginalized groups in ways that transform power relations for the benefit of sustainability and equity. These approaches emphasize the interplay between societal structures and views in bringing about transformative change, radically altering dominant social and human-nature relationships (Blaikie & Brookfield, 2015; Martinez-Alier, 2003; Woroniecki et al., 2019). Change arises through intentional actions and shifts in individual and collective agency (Gaventa, 2006; VeneKlasen, 2006).

Through critical self-awareness, engagement, resistance and protest, historically marginalized groups mobilize against underlying causes2 of biodiversity loss rooted in environmental injustices and entrenched powers to foster equitable and sustainable futures (Falla et al., 2024; Nightingale, 2017; Woroniecki, 2020). Transformative change manifests through new social arrangements, contested political spaces and empowered grassroots innovations that reconfigure dominant development trajectories and material flows (Drydyk, 2008; Eyben et al., 2006; Harcourt & Nelson, 2015) (Annex 3 .3). Theories within this approach include an emancipatory understanding of transformation linked to empowerment drawing on Paulo Freire’s (2000) notion of praxis, which is both a critique of existing social arrangements and a search for alternatives (Kabeer, 1999; Mehta et al., 2021). Theories in this approach emphasize values such as justice, equity and sustainability and focus on plurality2 and multiple dimensions of environmental justice (e.g., distributive, recognition and procedural) (Schlosberg, 2007, 2013; Temper, Demaria et al., 2018) as well as on the notion of capabilities (Nussbaum, 2002, 2011; Polishchuk & Rauschmayer, 2012; Sen, 2001, 2008). This approach envisages multiple means and actions for empowerment of actors (Stirling, 2015; Temper, Walter, et al., 2018). Mobilization and organization by Indigenous Peoples, local communities, minorities and other marginalized peoples can be a key feature of transformative change, through strategies such as lobbying, direct action, protest, strategic alliances with multiple actors and capacity-building (Ahmed, 2001; IPBES, 2023; Woroniecki et al., 2019). Other actions include fostering social movements and building grassroots networks, envisioning alternative pathways through participatory processes rooted in community ideas and values and work to gain recognition and representation in key arenas of power. During processes of transformative change, both individuals and diverse social groups acquire agency through collective action (McLaughlin & Dietz, 2008) in complex decision-making, bargaining and participatory processes. Bargaining, negotiation, non-action, resistance and reflection are important expressions of agency, in addition to decision-making (Kabeer, 1999; Manlosa, 2022). By centring the experiences, struggles and knowledge of Indigenous Peoples, women and other marginalized groups, empowerment approaches attempt to support diverse communities and peoples in their efforts to achieve meaningful participation in decision-making processes related to defining and implementing processes of transformative change (López-Serrano, 2023). These actors, often silenced or oppressed, emerge as key agents through participatory processes, grassroots innovations, collective actions, social movements (Mouffe, 2022) and ‘environmentalism of the poor’ (Martinez-Alier, 2003). By fostering critical thinking, dialogue and engagement with real-world problems, education based on deliberation and active participation can be a powerful tool for empowering marginalized groups (Freire & Macedo, 2005). The interplay of actors with institutions, policymakers and scientific communities through participatory, deliberative processes creates a dynamic force challenging existing power structures and enabling transformation. Through alternative practices, social innovations and visions in the making, these actors can address direct (e.g., land-use changes, climate change, pollution) and indirect (e.g., economy, values) drivers of biodiversity loss and nature’s decline (Avelino, 2021; Avelino et al., 2023).

Political ecology conceptualizes these activities as a driver of transformative change because it brings to light, politicizes and eventually overcomes prevailing social-ecological relationships (Blaikie & Brookfield, 2015; Peet & Watts, 2004). Actors in this approach include individuals and environmental justice, feminist, Indigenous and degrowth2 social movements against extractive unsustainable and capitalist-driven environment-development trajectories. Specific actions include those led to assert agency and address social, gender and environmental injustices, regain access to and control over the commons and natural resources which are key to sustaining their livelihoods, assert alternative visions to nature/human/more-than- human relations in decision-making spaces, and to reverse dominant systems of exploitation of nature and humans (Harcourt & Nelson, 2015; Temper, Walter, et al., 2018). In conclusion, transformative change, according to this approach, happens when marginalized people regain self- determination vis a vis dominant and exploitation power structures. Power is not simply power ‘over’ but also ‘power to’ and power ‘with’, power ‘within’ and power ‘for’ (Lécuyer et al., 2024; VeneKlasen & Miller, 2002). Through these reconfigurations of power, hitherto disempowered and marginalized groups use critical praxis, self-reflection, collective action and agency to gain concrete achievements through changing structures, asserting identities, gaining representation, recognition and rights in legal and other formal structures, often leading to better biodiversity outcomes (Annex 3 .3). 3.2.5 Knowledge co-creation approaches According to this approach, transformative change occurs collaboratively through the co-creation of knowledge on pathways, strategies and visions that spur transformative action (Ansell et al., 2022; Caniglia et al., 2020; Turnhout & Lahsen, 2022). This approach seeks to embed processes of societal change in careful, collaborative and socially- engaged knowledge production (Sellberg et al., 2021) by working at the interface of views and practices as key entry points to transformative change. Theories in this approach therefore call for a transformation in how research and education are produced and governed (Horcea-Milcu et al., 2024) and are explored further in Strategies 4 and 5 in Chapter 5. Knowledge co-creation-based approaches aim to improve the science-society interface and to better integrate knowledge within decision-making (Pascual, Balvanera, Anderson et al., 2023).

Examples under this approach are transdisciplinary projects (Lang et al., 2012), participatory action research (Arnstein, 1969; Blackstock et al., 2007), ethnoecology (Caillon et al., 2017; Gavin et al., 2015; Sabinot, 2021; Toledo & Alarcón-Cháires, 2012) and sustainability science (O’Brien, 2012; Pereira et al., 2019; Tengö et al., 2017) (Annex 3 .3). While participatory approaches and forms of participatory democracy have been around for a while in policy processes, typical theories within the knowledge co-creation approach envision that co-creation starts in a bottom-up manner from a science-society partnership led by academics and/or non-academics (e.g., municipality [Page 20] THE THEMATIC ASSESSMENT REPORT ON THE UNDERLYING CAUSES OF BIODIVERSITY LOSS, DETERMINANTS OF TRANSFORMATIVE CHANGE AND OPTIONS FOR ACHIEVING THE 2050 VISION FOR BIODIVERSITY 120 staff, civil society representatives, or community members), or even originating from grassroots movements (Ansell et al., 2022). Co-creation can emerge from hybrid alliances which bring the historically marginalized perspectives of Indigenous Peoples and other groups to the fore (Mehta et al., 2021). Co-creation may emerge from processes designed to imagine just and sustainable futures (visioning), develop alternative pathways towards these desirable futures or co-design context-specific and legitimate solution options (Chapter 2). Examples include the three-horizon technique (Sharpe et al., 2016) or arts-based methods. Examples of such experimental settings include place-based transdisciplinary fora, real-world laboratories, action-oriented projects in higher education and grassroots innovations. Co-creation promotes the expression of a plurality of actors’ agency as a critical ingredient in transformation. The knowledge co-creation process and actions pay attention to weaving knowledge from diverse academic and non-academic sources and to cultivating adaptability and emergence to the wants and needs of involved actors (Tengö et al., 2017, Aksoy and Öz, 2020). The co-creation process seeks to build individual and collective capacities to initiate or reinforce pathways and futures collectively deemed emancipatory and desirable. The outcomes of the co-creation process include capacity development, policy uptake, institution building, management practices, networking, reframing (e.g., problems, power, agency or solutions), empowerment and social equity (Chambers et al., 2021).

The outcomes of the co-creation process include capacity development, policy uptake, institution building, management practices, networking, reframing (e.g., problems, power, agency or solutions), empowerment and social equity (Chambers et al., 2021). Moreover, co-creation approaches can set the basis for actions and interventions grounded in other approaches (e.g., empowerment, inner transformation) by contributing to levelling out power asymmetries, expanding actors’ sense of agency and inner worlds and potentially improving social inclusion. Co-creation enables transformation by reframing conventional mainstream perspectives concerning biodiversity and valuation of ecosystem services2 to include, among others, marginalized and Indigenous perspectives. These include prior beliefs, assumptions and taken-for- granted perspectives on oneself, relationships with others and society. These standpoints are explored and sometimes confronted to evolve into more open, aware, collaborative and adaptable viewpoints, values and social practices. Visioning, dialogues, reflection and feedback sessions, including sharing knowledge in an accessible way, can all support this process. Various bodies of knowledge and research communities can bring their contributions to the co-creation process. For example, according to environmental history, deliberative transformative change can occur when all actors involved in an environmental conflict become aware of the role they have played in environmental degradation and this awareness is coupled with shared environmental memory transmitted through social communication and education which results in actions towards sustainable outcomes (Burke & Pomeranz, 2009; Gadgil & Guha, 1995). Under this approach, all actors relevant to the sustainability problem at hand are called to join forces in co-creating transformations. Inclusivity and plurality of knowledge systems are highly encouraged (Fazey et al., 2018; Norström et al., 2020), as long as there is transparency at the normative level. Depending on the context and on the problem constellation (Lam, Martín-López et al., 2021), examples of relevant actors are: Indigenous Peoples and local communities, local institutional actors, researchers from academic institutions, practitioners, policymakers in international, governmental and non-governmental organizations and industry, educators and students, media, workers and trade unions, citizens, non-human communities and the private sector. The diversity of actors brings different levels of power, dependence on nature’s contributions to people, experiences and expertise. Structured ways of involving diverse actors in co-creation processes (e.g., sequence of engagement methods and tools) can greatly facilitate co-creation approaches.

Science and technology approaches Under this approach, science and technology are seen as the primary drivers of transformative change. Theoretical frameworks in the science and technology approach suggest that production of scientific and technical knowledge on biodiversity, clean production technologies and the development of socio-technical infrastructures to address biodiversity loss and nature’s decline, are essential to bring about transformative change for a just and sustainable world. While frameworks within this approach typically focus on traditional technological advances, some include the scientific development of inclusive, deliberative and democratic innovation and knowledge processes (Annex 3 .3). The technological development and innovation that features in these theories often draws on traditional [Page 21] CHAPTER 3. HOW TRANSFORMATIVE CHANGE OCCURS 121 ecological knowledge, associated practices and biological resources that have been preserved and maintained through Indigenous and local knowledge. Science and technology approaches recognize that there is a close, two-way interaction between policy and innovation. Policy change can trigger innovation (e.g., when technology to advance solar panel development is supported by policies to promote renewable energy), while innovation itself can trigger policy change (e.g., the Montreal Protocol on Ozone Depletion was made possible by innovations allowing the exchange of chlorofluorocarbons for other technologies) (see Case 7 outlined in Annex 3 .1). Promoting transformative change through science and technology entails interactions with a diversity of actors who can take up innovations or novel technologies and spread them enough to be effective at generating transformative change (Heeks et al., 2013; Radjou et al., 2015). Innovation, according to the science and technology approach, can take several forms.

text: sformative change through science and technology entails interactions with a diversity of actors who can take up innovations or novel technologies and spread them enough to be effective at generating transformative change (Heeks et al., 2013; Radjou et al., 2015). Innovation, according to the science and technology approach, can take several forms. It can occur through conventional research, development, demonstration and diffusion policies. It can also be geared towards economic growth (Schumpeter, 1967), or emerge to respond to and address problems emanating from crisis, such as pandemics, socioeconomic inequalities and environmental problems. For example, agroecological transformations create integrated land-use systems that improve ecological processes and strengthen local communities, addressing problems emanating from conventional agricultural practices that rely on synthetic inputs and short-term productivity (Andrieu & Kebede, 2020). Innovation may also focus on policies or the creation of spaces for bottom-up innovation directed towards sustainability (Schot & Steinmueller, 2018). These innovations in socio-technical infrastructures and practices can provide opportunities for reshaping views and structures, such as ways of knowing and governance arrangements (Beaulieu, 2022) and thus facilitate other approaches such as structural or inner transformation approaches. Many theoretical frameworks in the science and technology approach focus on triggering transformative change via targeted funding for research to address environmental issues, support for environmentally driven start-ups and close collaboration between academia, government and the business sector to identify areas where science and technology can address sustainability problems. However, the theoretical frameworks within this approach span those that view science and technology as universalist and neutral, following a linear process from discovery to societal impact (Asafu-Adjaye et al., 2015), to approaches that emphasize the social and cultural embeddedness and political contingencies of science and technology (Bijker, 2017; Stokland et al., 2023; Turnhout, 2018), including the importance of institutional structures and power in shaping the distribution of benefits of technological advances (Johnson & Acemoglu, 2023). These different underlying assumptions about the role of science in transformation lead to a variety of recommended actions spanning from increased funding and political uptake and support for science and technology to more inclusive, just and deliberative processes for producing and employing it (Hausknost & Haas, 2019; Levidow & Papaioannou, 2018; Mazzucato, 2021).

Often ignored, but critically important, are Indigenous and local knowledge holders as a source of knowledge for science, technology and innovation regarding traditional knowledge, associated practices and biological resources that have been preserved and maintained through generations (Berkes, 2009, 2017; Kamau & Winter, 2013; Thrupp, 1989). Also critical are individuals who take up and use new technologies and innovations at scales sufficient to drive transformative change. Actions to promote transformative change, according to this approach, include increased public funding and provision of incentives for research, development (Mazzucato, 2013; Mazzucato & Semieniuk, 2017; Rodrik, 2015), demonstration and diffusion of technologies directed towards reducing biodiversity loss and nature’s decline; public funding for education in science and technology; the establishment of institutionalized channels for integrating scientific knowledge on biodiversity into policymaking at multiple scales (Haas, 1992, 2015), i.e., global or national; coordination of activities between different actors (the State, universities, business and others) (Schot & Steinmueller 2018)); provision of collective and inclusive spaces for learning and societal experimentation that allows for collaboration in setting the priorities for technology and innovation by various actors (Aksoy & Öz, 2020; Schot, 2002). The underlying causes of biodiversity loss and nature’s decline are not directly targeted in this approach. Rather, it seeks to directly address policies and practices that lead to biodiversity loss and nature’s decline; social and economic inequalities caused by disruptive production processes (Pansera & Owen, 2018); exclusionary innovations (Kaplinsky et al., 2009) and exploitative agriculture practices that reduce the natural capital of agroecosystems. At times, science and technology provide insights into the nature of the problem (for example whether chlorofluorocarbons affect the ozone layer or whether carbon emissions cause climate change) and then contribute to solutions through the development of new technologies and social innovations for consumption and improved monitoring capacities (e.g., machine learning processed satellite data).

Recent potentially transformative scientific and technological developments, such as artificial intelligence, digital innovations, synthetic biology and gene-editing technologies, provide crucial points of discussion on the role and impact of these emerging technologies on economic production, human well-being and sustainability (Clapp & Ruder, 2020; Erdmann et al., 2023; German Environment Agency & Federal Agency for Nature Conservation, 2024; Ingram & Maye, 2020; Johnson & Acemoglu, 2023; Luque-Ayala et al., 2024; Nicholson & Reynolds, 2020; Rabitz et al., 2022). 3.3 SYNTHESIS ACROSS THE APPROACHES Each of the six approaches focuses on particular dimensions or entry points for bringing about transformative change and tend to be embedded in different knowledge communities that often have limited interaction (Chapter 1). The focal entry points for each approach relate to the key challenges and underlying causes of biodiversity loss and nature’s decline perceived under each approach, which consequently highlight the most appropriate or powerful ways of initiating transformative change (i.e., their theory of change). In line with this, each of the approaches emphasizes particular types of actions (interventions) carried out by specific groups of actors (Table 3 .1).

In line with this, each of the approaches emphasizes particular types of actions (interventions) carried out by specific groups of actors (Table 3 .1). Indigenous and local knowledge contributes to all six approaches in different ways (Table 3 .1; Figure 3 .3). Importantly, because transformative change involves interconnected changes across views, structures and practices, the six approaches tend to complement and support one another when aligned around a common vision or purpose (Chapter 2). Promoting and accelerating transformative change is more likely when the different approaches are used in combinations that support one another. For example, it can be difficult to change practices without changing structures such as regulations, while structural change without changes in views can lead to resistance and protests (Riechers et al., 2022). There is no universal best entry point or approach for bringing about transformative change; the most appropriate entry points and most effective combination of approaches will depend on the context, including specific legacies, challenges and existing strengths and capacities of a particular system or place. Furthermore, the most appropriate sets of approaches are likely to change over time during different phases of a transformative change process. Taken together, the six approaches emphasize the diversity of actions and interventions by a diverse array of actors that can be used in complementary ways to initiate and navigate transformative change in different contexts (Figure 3 .4; Chapter 5). These key actions include: i) Systems: visioning, connecting change agents and shifting system feedbacks and interactions towards sustainable development pathways; ii) Structural: altering economic, social, political and cultural rules through governance interventions, market structures or communities reforming predominant rules; iii) Inner transformation: investing in relational activities that nurture human-other-than-human relationships, intra- and inter-generational relationships, self-other relationships and relationships with oneself leading to shifting inner beliefs, views and practices; iv) Empowerment: fostering social movements and building grassroot networks; to gain recognition, representation and rights in legal structures and other key arenas of power; v) Knowledge co-creation: investing in dialogue and opportunities for collaborative science-society initiatives; and vi) Science & technology: targeted funding and governmental support for research and development, innovation and technology and supporting the use of new technology and innovations.

Recognizing the diversity of approaches, entry points, actions and actors, as well as the diversity of contexts, there is no magic bullet approach to initiating transformative change. All pathways of transformative change involve multiple approaches, actors and actions that change over time (Box 3 .1, Figure 3 .4) and have different strengths and weaknesses (Table 3 .2). Pursuing transformative change entails choices and a recognition that many of these choices will result in some who benefit and some who pay the cost (and may resist change). Strengths Weaknesses Systems approaches Can help highlight system properties and actions that have greatest potential to leverage fundamental change . They tend to ignore issues of power, politics, social difference and intersectionality, which can perpetuate incumbent power relations and social inequalities . Structural approaches Emphasize the necessity to alter the social, legal, economic and political rules that uphold unsustainable practices . They have the potential to create changes in short timeframes by changing the rules for all . They tend to ignore aspects concerning human agency, culture and social differentiation . They assume that changes in social structures (e .g ., regulations, technologies) will shift individual behaviours, which is not always the case . Inner transformation approaches Capture the individual, relational and collective shift in values that can result in larger scale change . They do not require individuals to wait for structural change at other levels; each person can focus on themselves and their own abilities .

They can focus on the process of co-production2 rather than outcome, which can be slower than other ways to promote change . Attention to local knowledge makes these approaches context-dependent and difficult to scale up . Science-technology approaches Conventionally mirror the emergent technological changes that are often the feature of historical transformation (e .g ., the impact of railways on trade and resource management via the ability to move goods and the development of a common sense of time) . They can lead to a lack of diverse ways to address problems, especially if science and technology are seen as the sole solutions or if one technology becomes dominant at the expense of others . They can lead to quick fixes that overlook local complexities or solutions outside the science-technology space . [Page 25] CHAPTER 3. Creative and participatory arts-based and visual approaches have the potential to sketch vivencia (lived experiences; Glassman & Erdem, 2014) and can potentially open up new conversations that otherwise might be impeded by hierarchical social structures, such as caste traditions or gender inequities (Lewin & Shaw, 2021). Vulnerable and marginalized populations are often keepers of biodiversity due to their historically embedded and Indigenous understandings of and relationships to the sea, rivers, forests and deserts. Yet, they are often framed as recipients of policies rather than as active stakeholders. Arts-based methods seek to address these power imbalances and ensure that hidden, subaltern perspectives and situated knowledge (Haraway, 1988) remain central to research, policy and practice related to the conservation, restoration and sustainable use of biodiversity. Arts-based approaches can be used across all six clusters outlined in this chapter, but are most relevant for the empowerment, co-creation and inner transformation clusters and can unleash both cultural and structural changes. For example, in the TAPESTRY project (Tapestry Project, n.d.) researchers used arts-based methods to unearth implicit narratives and stories from the vantage point of islanders from the Bangladesh and Indian Sundarbans, the world’s largest mangrove delta. Using photovoice (Photovoice With Pastoralists, n.d.), researchers were able to look through the lens of the communities (Bose et al., 2023). The project also enabled researchers to look at the world with the imaginative gaze of the children through their paintings (Barton, 2015).

Another example of the transformative potential of arts- based methods comes from urban Mumbai, where coastal ecosystems and wetlands (e.g., mangrove forests and biodiversity creeks) have been systematically appropriated by the State and private actors for commercial and infrastructure development purposes (Movik et al., 2023). Combined with pollution, sea-level rise and coastal erosion, these factors have had very adverse impacts on fish stocks and the livelihoods of artisanal Koli fishers, the original and Indigenous inhabitants of Mumbai. Photovoice and place- making activities helped bring forward visual representations of contested coastal environments and how Kolis live. Livelihoods are closely linked with the sea, creeks and mangroves and their destruction and appropriation threaten the future of the Kolis, while undermining marine biodiversity and coastal resilience (see collection of photos below; Bose et al., 2018; Segovia & Hervé, 2022). Creative, visual and arts-based approaches can explore the intersections of the human/non-human, State/community and the productive/care economy and how these are negotiated by local communities such as pastoralists, artisanal fishers and forest-dependent communities and what these mean for their sense of culture, place and identity (Segovia & Hervé, 2022).

[Page 32] THE THEMATIC ASSESSMENT REPORT ON THE UNDERLYING CAUSES OF BIODIVERSITY LOSS, DETERMINANTS OF TRANSFORMATIVE CHANGE AND OPTIONS FOR ACHIEVING THE 2050 VISION FOR BIODIVERSITY 132 3.5 KEY INSIGHTS ON HOW TRANSFORMATIVE CHANGE OCCURS There is at present no scientific consensus or a single agreed-upon theory for how transformative change leading to a sustainable future occurs. Rather, there is a diverse and extensive body of literature that spans many disciplines and areas of study and provides different insights on the process of transformative change and how it is initiated, promoted and scaled (Annex 3 .3). Six broad approaches were identified (systems, structural, inner transformations, empowerment, knowledge co-creation and science and technology) and have underlying commonalities in their views of how transformative change occurs and the key actions and actors that can bring about change (Section 3 .2). Each of the approaches can be linked to particular focal entry points of views, structures, practices or combinations of these (Figure 3 .1). There is currently no “meta-theory” of transformative change that synthesizes across the six approaches (Section 3 .7). However, a one-dimensional approach to transformative change is insufficient and there is no single best approach to initiating transformative change. Rather, promoting and accelerating transformative change is more likely when the different approaches are used in combinations that support one another and are suited to a particular context and point in time of a transformative change process. Historical examples show that transformative change on the scale needed to address biodiversity loss and nature’s decline has occurred multiple times throughout history and is possible. Although most of these historic changes have been detrimental to biodiversity (e.g., Industrial Revolution) (Box 3 .3), they provide important insights about the dynamics and processes of the fundamental, system-wide transformative change needed to halt the loss of biodiversity and nature’s decline.

Although most of these historic changes have been detrimental to biodiversity (e.g., Industrial Revolution) (Box 3 .3), they provide important insights about the dynamics and processes of the fundamental, system-wide transformative change needed to halt the loss of biodiversity and nature’s decline. At the same time, ongoing initiatives from around the world provide promising examples of transformative change at local to regional scales that have the potential to inform and contribute to system-wide change at the scale needed to halt the loss of biodiversity and nature’s decline (Section 3 .4, Box 3 .1). Box 3 3 Historical case study: the Industrial Revolution – an example of the potential scale and magnitude of the transformative changes needed to address biodiversity loss and nature’s decline . The magnitude of change that occurred during the Industrial Revolution mirrors the scale and scope of transformation that many experts believe will be needed to achieve global environmental sustainability (Linnér & Wibeck, 2019a). During the Industrial Revolution, multiple changes of varying scales across time and place combined and cascaded to result in global transformative change that influenced almost every aspect of daily life. Transformation on such a massive scale, even if not focused on sustainability, can help to illustrate how each of the approaches to transformation identified in this chapter understands how transformation occurs and the contribution and insights they have to offer in bringing about transformative change. This example also highlights how any single theory or approach misses key aspects of transformative change and thus emphasizes the importance of using multiple theories together to understand, promote and navigate transformative change. As with most examples of transformative change, the Industrial Revolution grew out of other large changes. The scientific revolution and the Enlightenment, themselves traced back to inner transformation and Descartes’ mind-body theory, have been argued to be prime drivers of the Industrial Revolution (Linnér & Wibeck, 2019a). In terms of views, the scientific revolution and the Enlightenment have been argued to be prime drivers of the Industrial Revolution, promoting the idea that empirical knowledge and reason could be used to understand and control nature2, which was increasingly viewed in terms of instrumental values, rather than relational values or intrinsic values2. These visions2 and their increasing uptake among people, began a shift from a relational worldview to one based on reason and individualism2 that represents a dramatic shift in human consciousness (Hamilton, 2002). This aspect highlights the catalytic role that inner transformations (Section 3 .2 .3) can play in promoting change to a different type of future.

The Industrial Revolution can also be understood as a prime example of ‘science and technology’ approaches (Section 3 .2 .6), where knowledge delivers new technologies that are then taken up by society at scale. In this case, the new knowledge and technologies included the coal-fired steam engine and textile machinery, which enabled vast increases in speed and efficiency of production, leading to a transformation in how nearly every product is made and deep changes in how people work and how society is organized (Allen, 2019). Although differing from modern perspectives on knowledge co- creation, the sources of knowledge for the Industrial Revolution reflect co-creation as defined by the creation of value by a variety of actors outside mainstream knowledge producers (Section 3 .2 .5). Inventors from a range of backgrounds contributed to the technological innovation that marks the Industrial Revolution, including those from ‘humble origins’. This occurred even though at the time Britain was an oligarchic society where merit was seen as causally related to inherited [Page 33] CHAPTER 3. HOW TRANSFORMATIVE CHANGE OCCURS 133 Box 3 3 social class (Cardwell, 2019; Khan, 2018) and people of ‘humble origins’ were marginalized. Structural approaches (Section 3 .2 .2), focusing on theories about the importance of the reorganization of production and the role of finance and the economy, also help highlight and explain many changes at the heart of the Industrial Revolution. Each new technology allowed greater exploitation of nature and the increasing efficiency rewarded and funded further development and greater profit. European empires extended in the search for natural resources2 and people, to exploit and accumulate wealth. This created substantial inequalities in power relations2, including class inequities and different impacts across geographies in the form of colonialism2. Many of these inequalities persist today and empowerment approaches (Section 3 .2 .4) highlight addressing these as central to tackling the root causes of biodiversity loss and nature’s decline. Finally, ideas deemed important by systems approaches (Section 3 .2 .1), such as the role of interactions among different parts of the system, were key factors in the Industrial Revolution. The Industrial Revolution involved a paradigm shift in human-nature relations that provided a new vision of a better future, which was reinforced by new technologies across different places and new societal structures and practices that reinforced and accelerated the changes (Christensen, 1962; Homer & Alfred, 1982).

The Industrial Revolution involved a paradigm shift in human-nature relations that provided a new vision of a better future, which was reinforced by new technologies across different places and new societal structures and practices that reinforced and accelerated the changes (Christensen, 1962; Homer & Alfred, 1982). The paradox for the current assessment is that the Industrial Revolution had substantial and widespread negative consequences for biodiversity and ecosystems as demand for raw materials grew. The exponential growth in human population (Annex 3 .1) required vast increases in food production (Tostevin, 2014). The Industrial Revolution is thus associated with an exploitative relationship with nature, with Descartes writing that science allowed humans to be masters and possessors of nature (Merrill, 2008). The intention for change, desire to break free from the bonds of nature and the belief that separation from nature is possible can be seen in the writings of key figures from that time. For example, Francis Bacon, a key figure in the scientific revolution, asserted that humans have power, command, dominion and rights over nature by divine request. Sigmund Freud also wrote about humans coming together and ‘taking up the attack on nature, thus forcing it to obey human will, under the guidance of science’ (Kidner, 1994). These shifts in thinking are now being questioned and challenged when dealing with the far-reaching consequences they have had for nature and human societies. The essential lesson that the Industrial Revolution offers for navigating transformative change is that all six broad approaches are helpful in understanding how transformative change occurs, as they highlight different aspects of transformative change processes. No one approach on its own captures the complex, multi-dimensional nature of transformative change. Rather, all six approaches provide important insights into promoting and navigating transformative change at large, systemic scales and combining insights across different approaches provides the best basis for understanding how transformative change may be promoted and accelerated across diverse contexts and scales. These examples emphasize that transformative change is rarely the outcome of a single event or driver and is better understood as a pathway or process of change involving multiple cascading changes that trigger and reinforce one another, often in unexpected ways (Chapter 1; Sections 3 .2 and 3 .3; Box 3 .1). This section synthesizes key insights about how transformative change occurs, as evidenced by the six broad approaches to transformative change, historical case studies of transformative change and insights from the database of local and regional examples.

This section synthesizes key insights about how transformative change occurs, as evidenced by the six broad approaches to transformative change, historical case studies of transformative change and insights from the database of local and regional examples. 3.5.1 Insight 1: Weaving together diverse knowledges and approaches The first insight is that transformative change typically involves weaving together actions and changes that draw on multiple approaches and ways of knowing (Figure 3 .8). Different approaches highlight different entry points for bringing about transformative change, with the most appropriate entry points dependent on the context. Transformative change involves mutually reinforcing change across a broad set of views, structures and practices (Chapter 1). Attention to synergies2 among different approaches and pathways of change can build and accelerate enduring transformative change (Eakin et al., 2021; Waddock, 2023). Without such reinforcement, change is likely to be narrower, less transformative and with greater risk of resistance (Sections 3 .5 .3 and 3 .5 .5; Chapter 4). Attention to a single transformative change approach, such as the structure of the system or empowering people, risks backsliding and failing to lead to true transformation (Chapter 1). Indeed, transformative change at the scale needed to meet global sustainability goals for biodiversity and human well-being is likely to involve the incorporation of all six approaches, applied or integrated to different extents in different places, times and contexts. No one approach on its own is likely to be sufficient to promote and navigate large-scale transformations to sustainability. For instance, a local innovation based on a technological advance co- created between local actors can reduce biodiversity loss [Page 34] THE THEMATIC ASSESSMENT REPORT ON THE UNDERLYING CAUSES OF BIODIVERSITY LOSS, DETERMINANTS OF TRANSFORMATIVE CHANGE AND OPTIONS FOR ACHIEVING THE 2050 VISION FOR BIODIVERSITY 134 and nature’s decline (Mehta et al., 2021). However, such an innovation also needs wider structural and institutional change, as well as political buy-in to gain wider acceptability or be scaled up (Nishi et al., 2021). The most appropriate entry points and approaches will depend on the context. Change towards transformation may start with concerted intervention at a particular entry point that aligns with one approach that fits a particular context and continue with actions and interventions drawing on other approaches and targeting other aspects of views, structures and practices. For example, in many contexts, a science and technology-based intervention or practice (e.g., the introduction of smartphones) may initiate change, while other approaches such as co-creation and empowerment may be more suited for navigating the process of change once started.

This knowledge often emphasizes responsibility, reciprocity and connectedness and has the potential to inform and inspire strategies and actions to fundamental, system-wide transformative change. Indigenous and local knowledge is made up of diverse worldviews that offer alternative ways of knowing and thinking about human-nature relationships that can help move from dominant modern worldviews characterized by utility, control and the separation of human and nature (Artelle et al., 2018; Choy, 2018; Sabinot & Lescureux, 2019; Toledo & Barrera Bassols, 2008). In contrast to modern worldviews that emphasize a rigid dichotomy between nature and culture, mind and matter and subject and object, Indigenous and local knowledge emphasizes the relational ontologies, which recognize the mutually constitutive relationships between human and more-than- human entities (Escobar, 2016; Lescureux, 2006), often featuring a whole and interconnected world of balance and harmony. For instance, Indigenous recognition of rights of nature and assertions of nature’s agency have given rise to a novel legal concept of legal personhood to non- human entities (Hutchison, 2014), creating an alternative to dominant anthropocentric approaches to legal structures (Charpleix, 2018; Kauffman & Martin, 2018; Martínez & Acosta, 2017) (Box 3 .1). Indigenous and local knowledge plays critical roles in bringing about transformative change towards sustainability across the multiple different approaches discussed in this chapter (Brondízio, Aumeeruddy-Thomas, et al. 2021; Reyes-García et al., 2022; Section 3 .2, Table 3 .1). Because of its place-based character (Lam, Hinz, et al., 2020), Indigenous and local knowledge can contribute to more plural transformations through knowledge co-creation approaches (Burgos-Ayala et al., 2020; Caillon et al., 2017; Fernández-Llamazares & Cabeza, 2018), where multiple knowledge sources and systems are engaged in weaving creative and innovative solutions for sustainability (Section 3 .2 .5, Box 3 .2). It also plays a prominent role in inner transformation approaches by shedding light on spiritual, emotional, cultural, social and historical dimensions of self- other relationships that can help trigger and leverage inner potentials for transformative change (Redvers et al., 2022; Wildcat, 2022) (Section 3 .2 .3).

The role of Indigenous and local knowledge in empowerment and structural approaches highlights political and management actions that can be taken to support transformative change. Supporting the agency, power and rights of Indigenous Peoples and local communities who have been holding, practicing and transmitting Indigenous and local knowledge over generations but have often been historically marginalized, can support stewardship activities associated with livelihoods and customary practices (Reyes- García et al., 2022; Rights and Resource Initiative, 2017). This can also develop and enhance capacities to engage in transformative pathways, as shown in the example of Udege People (Annex 3 .1), where transformation required new capacities in existing governance structures and powerful actors2 whose perspectives and routines are persistent. Within the context of structural approaches, Indigenous and local knowledge perspectives help to develop and improve principles, frameworks, agreements, rules and legislation as well as economic, social, political and cultural structures to acknowledge, appreciate, respect, preserve and maintain Indigenous and local knowledge and associated agency, [Page 36] THE THEMATIC ASSESSMENT REPORT ON THE UNDERLYING CAUSES OF BIODIVERSITY LOSS, DETERMINANTS OF TRANSFORMATIVE CHANGE AND OPTIONS FOR ACHIEVING THE 2050 VISION FOR BIODIVERSITY 136 rights and practices of Indigenous Peoples and local communities (Brondízio & Le Tourneau, 2016). It is important not only to recognize, understand and reflect on Indigenous and local knowledge, but also to disseminate such knowledge and visions of alternative futures to the broader population, for instance through education curricula, in order to attain broader political support. 3.5.3 Insight 3: Envisioning and growing sustainable futures The third insight is that visions play a powerful role in transformative change by giving space for imagination, providing inspiration, motivating collective action and reshaping behaviour at both individual and societal scales (Chapter 2). They can be used to disrupt the views, structures and practices that have led to the current crisis and to expand and embed equitable and sustainable alternatives. Transformative change implies a willingness to experiment and do things differently (Pereira, Hichert et al., 2018). Approaches that reinforce or conform to existing challenges and their manifestations constitute complexes of interrelated values, ontologies, behaviour, knowledges, extraction and production practices, government institutions, regulations and actor networks (Amel et al., 2017; Boström et al., 2018; Heyen & Wolff, 2019; Sewell, 2005).

Approaches that reinforce or conform to existing challenges and their manifestations constitute complexes of interrelated values, ontologies, behaviour, knowledges, extraction and production practices, government institutions, regulations and actor networks (Amel et al., 2017; Boström et al., 2018; Heyen & Wolff, 2019; Sewell, 2005). These current conditions are entrenched and hard to change for a number of reasons, including their complex interdependencies; powerful actors and institutions that profit from the status quo and resist change (Visseren-Hamakers et al., 2021); and partly because of the lack of clear visions and imaginations of viable alternative ways of living (E. Bennett et al., 2016; Martin et al., 2022). These relationships can be questioned and new approaches can be nurtured. A number of theories highlight the critical role of visions and imagination in deliberately engaging in processes of transformative change (Chapter 2). Imagining alternative possible futures can inform policy, mobilize resources, inspire individual agency and collective action and reshape behaviour at both individual and societal scales (Mansur et al., 2022; Moore & Milkoreit, 2020; Riedy & Waddock, 2022; Stoetzler & Yuval-Davis, 2002) (Section 3 .2). Feminist political ecologists have argued for the importance of imagination to enact desired relations, exchanges and values in the present, recognizing the histories of injustice and environmental harm that shape the future and kinship with all of life (Gergan, 2020; Lyons, 2023). However, many current policy targets reveal an imagination gap (Chapter 2), as they are based on implicit futures that largely assume a continuation of the status quo, with solutions to current sustainability crises revolving around narrow scientific and economic directions (McPhearson et al., 2021; Swilling, 2013) (Chapter 1). Carefully designed participatory imagination processes can build alternative, more diverse, collectively-owned visions (Box 3 .2, Annex 3 .1; Chapter 2), drawing on and integrating knowledge co-creation, empowerment and systems approaches to transformative change. Such alternative visions are increasingly seen as critical to developing shared future goals and understanding what needs to change, as well as to mobilizing the collective action and resources needed to achieve transformative change (E. Bennett et al., 2016; Lembi et al., 2024; Martin et al., 2022). Disruption of unsustainable views, structures and practices can be achieved in different ways, but often entails targeting systems of power relationships (Linnér & Wibeck, 2019b; Luederitz et al., 2017; Scoones et al., 2020; Sewell, 2005; Temper, Walter et al., 2018). Transformation is not an end state, rather it is a radical reshaping of current social, political, economic-environmental relations through which change occurs (Di Chiro, 2021; Lyons, 2023).

They can be powerfully used in participatory processes to build shared visions, understanding of a system and the critical areas in need of change by providing symbolic stories that support agency and actions towards making imagined futures real (Pereira, Hichert, et al., 2018; Sharpe et al., 2016). 3.5.4 Insight 4: Navigating tensions, trade-offs and conflicts The fourth insight is that transformative change challenges prevailing distributions of power and implies navigation of tensions, trade-offs and conflicts to gain the support of those who perceive themselves to be negatively affected by change. While decision makers may wish for smooth and non-contentious processes of change, research on transformations has highlighted that these processes typically involve intense power struggles (Moser, 2016). Deep, structural transformation often entails challenging power structures that perpetuate inequality2, dominant knowledge framings that ignore or oppress Indigenous and alternative pathways and perpetuate unsustainable patterns of resource use, consumption and production and the structural roots of vulnerability (Fischer, 2021). Different actors have different stakes in and experiences of transformative change due to their different entitlements, access to resources, worldviews, beliefs and norms (Fisher et al., 2022; O’Brien, 2018). Not all individuals and groups will benefit in the same way, or even benefit at all from transformative change (Box 3 .4, Annex 3 .1). Different types of contestations could be faced by those who are disempowered by the change and lack the power to be adaptive, but also by those with power who benefit from present structures and those who benefit from the change yet may lose power and influence (Berbés-Blázquez et al., 2016). Incumbents that benefit from the status quo may be deeply resistant to the emergence of new systems that question or overhaul incumbent interests and stakes (Moser, 2016; Visseren-Hamakers et al., 2021). Resistance may also emerge when people feel their identities or ways of life are threatened (Bourdieu, 1998; Scott, 1990).

Incumbents that benefit from the status quo may be deeply resistant to the emergence of new systems that question or overhaul incumbent interests and stakes (Moser, 2016; Visseren-Hamakers et al., 2021). Resistance may also emerge when people feel their identities or ways of life are threatened (Bourdieu, 1998; Scott, 1990). This may be aggravated by historical legacies of power hierarchies, politics, exclusions and injustices around race, class, gender, caste, ethnicity and resource grabbing that have led to the silencing of the voices, needs and interests of Indigenous and local actors and their relationships with their ecosystems (Abu-Lughod, 1990; Awasis, 2023). This can lead to significant tensions in the process of transformative change and amongst different options for pathways of change, each of which will have a range of positive and negative impacts for different actors (Blythe et al., 2018; Martin et al., 2024). Power is implicit in all systems and structures, but it is rarely recognized and targeting structural power can be very difficult, but potentially transformative (Arias-Arévalo et al., 2023; Lécuyer et al., 2024). Knowing where power lies, how it works and how to make use of its vulnerabilities is essential to transforming unsustainable systems and structures. Targeting tensions between actors and different pathways of change can also foster opportunities for learning. These conflicts can also themselves be triggers of social transformation (Dahlet et al., 2021). Some tensions, trade-offs and conflicts can be mediated through dialogue and by ensuring that all actors are included in transformative change processes through processes of empowerment (Section 3 .2 .4) and knowledge co-creation (Section 3 .2 .5). While the dominant science and technology- focused approaches to transformation (Section 3 .2 .6) in the past have largely privileged ‘experts’ (scientists and policymakers), increasingly, a range of approaches emphasize that everybody has a role in sustainability transformations (Sections 3 .2, 3 .3, 3 .4), especially marginalized groups and Indigenous Peoples and local communities who are often denied voice and agency in such processes (Brondízio & Le Tourneau, 2016). Just and equitable transformations emphasize the importance of addressing the needs of the disempowered (N. Bennett et al., 2019). 3.5.5 Insight 5: Everyone can contribute The fifth insight is that a wide variety of actors, including individuals, groups and formal institutions, are able to initiate and contribute to transformative change. Different actors have different spheres of influence2 that interact and are dynamic (Berdegué et al., 2015). Successful transformative change is often realized by diverse actor coalitions that bring together complementary resources, capacities and approaches.

Different actors have different spheres of influence2 that interact and are dynamic (Berdegué et al., 2015). Successful transformative change is often realized by diverse actor coalitions that bring together complementary resources, capacities and approaches. The underlying causes of biodiversity loss and nature’s decline (Chapter 1) and the challenges to transformative change (Chapter 4) are significant, cross- scalar and interrelated. Transformative change involves addressing these causes and challenges in an integrative manner, as emphasized especially by systems approaches (Section 3 .2 .1). Actor coalitions therefore play an important role in successful examples of transformative change (Enfors-Kautsky et al., 2021) (Section 3 .4). The formation of actor coalitions and networks can be facilitated by high-quality knowledge co-creation [Page 39] CHAPTER 3. HOW TRANSFORMATIVE CHANGE OCCURS 139 approaches (Keck & Sikkink, 1998a, 1998b; Rogowski, 1990; Sabatier, 1998) (Section 3 .2 .5) particularly if they pay attention to issues of power and are aligned with the principles of equity and justice, pluralism and inclusion, respectful and reciprocal human-nature relationships and adaptive learning and action. Actor coalitions are most successful when there is an alignment of values and interests (Sabatier & Weible, 2007; Sell & Prakash, 2004). Visioning processes that lead to jointly owned and agreed- upon future visions can facilitate the identification and development of shared values and interests and can be powerful in bringing together diverse groups, including those that may be in conflict (Kahane, 2004) (Chapter 2). Research on social change highlights how the aggregation of distributed actions by individuals and institutions have contributed to transformative changes (Finnemore & Sikkink, 1998). Social movements often work for changes in structures (ways of organizing, regulating, governing) and many initiatives also focus on changing social and cultural norms (ways of doing, behaving, relating). Transformation can be fostered or nudged both through formal and informal strategies and through transformative alliances and knowledge co-creation between diverse actors that come together to co-produce transformative change and reconfigure relationships of power and knowledge (Annex 3 .3). Such collective agency is a crucial form of power for breaking down old systems and creating new systems (Charli-Joseph et al., 2018, 2023; Otto et al., 2020). Collective agency occurs when people act together, such as in social movements (Caniglia et al., 2020; Falla et al., 2024). Collective agency is situational; it is not held by groups but empowered through the relationships and resources available to actors. Enabling diverse forms of agency, especially from below, can be very powerful and build momentum for transformative change (Section 3 .2 .4).
